Anna Moneymaker | Getty Images Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected. Shares of the bank fell more than 7% in premarket trading. Here's what the company reported: Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEG Revenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEG The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share. Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance. 'Worst in class' In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter. Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate. The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, will inevitably spark questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets. Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Now, questions arise as to whether there are any more risk-management issues waiting to be found. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, adds 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. Gerry Miller | CNBC Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the company reported: Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimate Revenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Morgan Stanley cited widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower IPOs and a decline in fixed income underwriting. Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. headlines.article_text: BlackRock draws $205 billion in client funds as quarterly profit beats estimates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article BLK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The BlackRock logo is pictured outside the company's headquarters in the Manhattan borough of New York City on May 25, 2021. Carlo Allegri | Reuters BlackRock surpassed Wall Street profit expectations and attracted $205 billion in total inflows in the third quarter, sending the world's largest asset manager's shares up 5% in premarket trading on ⁠Wednesday. The benchmark S&P 500 extended its steady climb in the quarter to hover near its all-time highs on a rally in AI-focused ​stocks, encouraging investors to pour ​money into asset management firms ​such as BlackRock. "Market fundamentals are strong and well supported, with higher margins and earnings momentum catalyzed by new technology," CEO Larry Fink said in a statement. BlackRock's assets under management — which determine a large chunk of the earnings — ⁠rose ‌to $15.49 trillion, from $13.46 trillion a year earlier and $15.34 trillion ⁠in the second quarter. The growth was driven by a combination of $134.5 billion of new flows into BlackRock's flagship iShares ETFs, and the rising valuations of its investments in a robust equity market. The company posted an adjusted profit of $15.93 per share, beating Wall Street ‌expectations of $14.13, according to data compiled by LSEG. The robust results will help alleviate pressure on BlackRock's shares, which have underperformed the broader market this year over fears of a slowdown in ​activity from cautious investor sentiment. Even as markets have remained sturdy, the combination of surging bond yields and the expectation that the Federal Reserve's recent interest rate hike marks the beginning of a tightening cycle has called into question whether the rally can be sustained. Higher yields over a ⁠sustained period can put pressure on markets as investors rotate capital into safe-haven assets, locking in better risk-adjusted returns. Net flows into ‌BlackRock's debt products were $78.2 billion in the quarter, signaling strong investor ‌appetite despite the recent steep selloff in Treasuries. Redemptions ease in private credit BlackRock has accelerated its push into private credit markets in recent years.
